title: Which game genres are the hardest to develop, even with AI assistance?
author: dnr424
selftext:
AI tools are making game development a lot easier these days, but I'm guessing some genres are still pretty tough to pull off.

Which genres do you think are the hardest to develop, even with AI helping with coding and other stuff?

comments.author: zayelion
comments.body: FPS, MMOs, anything multiplayer.

replies.author: Evening_Till_3779
replies.body: They're actually really good at multiplayer stuff though?

comments.author: Bonelessgummybear
comments.body: I'd say RTS and Mobas, simply because of balancing and play testing. I believe I can generate and animate the entire game though. Open world games that don't feel empty would be up there too. Both are definitely possible though, I have a RTS idea stashed away for the right moment

replies.author: niloony
replies.body: There's a flood of RTS-like games on social media with massive traction at the moment. It doesn't matter if they're balanced if you can get player fantasy going.

replies.author: Putrid_Clue_2127
replies.body: I actually didn't know that. I've been working on my own rts-adjacent type game for mobile and didn't realize there was a flood of this genre happening right now. I mostly set out to make it because it's what I've always wanted in a game myself, but now I'm wondering if it'll actual gain any traction with others. Oh well, a couple hundred hours in, and probably a couple hundred more to go! It's been a fun journey either way.

replies.author: niloony
replies.body: 4x, Total war clones etc are all suffering the same thing. The technical moat they had has largely been filled in. Might be similar to when Unity got to a decent state and genres like platformer got crushed.

replies.author: Meatt
replies.body: Like what? Just curious, I'm currently making something near the genre, maybe I could plan for mobile as well.

replies.author: niloony
replies.body: Ebbtide, Defilade, Warfront, Burn It Back. That's just off the top of my head. The moat has been filled in for the genre so it's going to get crowded.

comments.author: hello-xworld
comments.body: RPGs and story driven games like visuals novels. AI is not great at storytelling yet imo, and this is where human creativity still shines.

replies.author: TheBigQuestion354
replies.body: Making an RPG currently. Would actually argue that now RPG's are much easier to make since you can spend much of the day writing the stories, quests, and characters yourself since AI handles most of the other work. Totally agree though that AI is not good at writing stories or characters.

replies.author: hello-xworld
replies.body: Definitely. I meant moreso using AI for the storyline since most RPGs are story driven. I’m also making an action RPG game and its helped me a lot making the actual game so I can focus on the story and narrative

replies.author: NightMailworks
replies.body: Yeah, the gulf between coding ability and good writing still surprises me.

replies.author: Arcodiant
replies.body:
If LLMs have one big weakness, it's that they'll return the most probable answer in most cases. For coding, you want that - you're not looking for a unique solution, you're looking for a correct solution.

But if you're writing a story, you don't want to get the same, most-common answers whenever you ask "who's the villain?" and "what's the twist?", you want something that fits but is original each time. I'm doing some work on how to seed LLMs with original directions, but it's a fight every step of the way.

replies.author: UncleJoesLandscaping
replies.body:
Agree. I am making an RPG and let Claude and ChatGPT have a shot at the story. The drivel that came out is something a 12 year old would turn in as their school assigment. The rediculous "fantasy names" they love sounded so bad I just wanted to adress NPCs by their titles.

Not all RPGs have to be story heavy though.

replies.author: TheBigQuestion354
replies.body: I wouldn’t even compare it to a 12 year old. It mostly just lore dumps the character like if you ask it to make an inn keeper with a mysterious secret the literal opening dialogue it will write will be “hello and welcome to the inn, my name is Adrianna and I secretly murder people but that wouldn’t be fair to share with you.”

replies.author: Ok-Investment4414
replies.body: u expect it to do so with 0 input, ai excels at this with input and examples

replies.author: revel911
replies.body:
That depends on the part. You could easily sketch the base of each story and have AI fill in the blanks.

Problem is people don't want to the leg work

"Here is my decision tree!" is way less cool than "look at my shiny, but thin demo."

comments.author: EdOfO
comments.body:
Simulation games (political, economic, social, cultural, specific topic)  
You can't fake the knowledge.
  
Games with good stories  
You can't fake writing talent.  
  
Strategy & fighting games  
They require fine-tuning balance between characters and classes.  
  
Anything that requires a considerable server backend or any significant anti-cheat  
You need more than AI code.

replies.author: Evening_Till_3779
replies.body:
>Simulation games (political, economic, social, cultural, specific topic)  
You can't fake the knowledge.

How is that true at all? Exactly the kind of thing AIs are good at, they know all that stuff

replies.author: Kind-Recording3450
replies.body: Simulation games they are good at but you need to feed it and correct it.

replies.author: marcosama
replies.body: Fighting games have so much meticulous tuning and animations to work through. Really needs a human eye to pull that off well.

replies.author: NeatEmergency725

comments.author: marcosama
comments.body: I imagine visual novels would be awful if humans aren't writing the dialogue or drawing the art lol!

comments.author: Baalzeg
comments.body: MMORPG. Requieres muchísimo conocimiento del género. Aún con IA la Iteración y el balance requieren cientos de pruebas para pulir la experiencia. Llevo casi 1 año creando uno, y es auténticamente difícil.

comments.author: SoullessGamesDev
comments.body: I think of anything that requires good 3d graphics and animations. Don't even know how to approach that with AI, i saw certain services that do 3d models, but not very good, and they are quite expencive. Animations? Have no idea. And you also need to put all of that in game somehow...

replies.author: AdagioElectrical3599
replies.body: I started looking at Tripo for 3d models and it seems quite good, but yeah, the animation and natural posing has a long way to go. You can tell in every game made by AI the weapon holding is always strange like it can’t get it quite right

replies.author: DazedGenie
replies.body:
As someone who has tried tripo and meshy I personally just prefee claude running a headless blender once taught properly can actually output some pretty decent 3d models. These are some of the ships Claude made in blender for me from an original piece of concept art and about 4 concept boat images. The system then can make any boat I want fairly easily. Models seen here are roughly 15-35k triangles each

https://i.redd.it/a3xonutc2e1i1.png

replies.author: SoullessGamesDev
replies.body: Thing with AI, it can look good from distance. But let's say i am making Resident Evil type of game, will every monster, character, and object from envoronment be both photorealistic and without obvious visual flaws when observed up close? I kinda doubt it.

replies.author: DazedGenie
replies.body:
Well that's what iteration is for. If you think your gonna get a perfect model the first time not sure what you really expect. The strongest part of ai is the ability to iterate with it. Obviously you have to adjust your process for what works for you and what you are making specifically. My game is mainly isometric so these work exceptionally well for what I want to do. Are there still issues with some of the rigging and what not? Absolutely but for my use case I've found them easier to work with, better for what I want, far more modular, and significantly cheaper than using a tripo or Meshy which I actually switched away from. Also I think the difference is you want photorealism. Obviously that is a much larger task than my cartoonish boats but that I feel like now we are talking about models vs the texture of those models. You can get good usable models out of just running blender but it is a lot of work and iteration but that is true about traditional modeling as well 🤷

https://i.redd.it/yjkji8jd6e1i1.png

replies.author: SoullessGamesDev
replies.body: Yeah, i think you are right, i worded my explanation poorly.

comments.author: teapot_RGB_color
comments.body:
Its not about genre, its more about scale.

So the correct answer here is Open-World and MMORPG.

  
While AI knows a lot about the subject from an outside view in, they have a lot less understanding of the subject itself. So much an American administration, you'll end up with the "concept" of an open world, a the concept of an mmorpg.

Getting something that would ever pass through a commercial gate for approval, in those genres, will have you rip your hair out trying to navigate through the hazards of optimization and context related design decisions.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body: Scale is no longer the problem, I can just hire more agents. Quality is the problem no matter the genre and hubris of new Devs.

comments.author: JorgitoEstrella
comments.body: MMORPG, first person rpg, whatever genre Warcraft 3 is.

comments.author: ckn
comments.body: I think the 80/20 rule, in general any game that involves its fanbase is the most difficult to develop.

comments.author: kultcher
comments.body: Anything that requires intricate level design, like games with multi-step spatial puzzles.

comments.author: Embarrassed-Crow9283
comments.body:
I don't think it's the genre that decides the difficulty. 

I don't think it's the game development that is hard. Sometimes it's incredibly expensive, but a lot of the successful games like Flappy Bird or Minecraft are doable in a few days or less for a decent game dev. 

Rather, it's designing what people want. That is the very hard thing, AI or not.

comments.author: Sikerow
comments.body: Actual content. Most "games" we see is a singular mechanic in good graphics. Because of the graphics it looks more impressive than it actually is

comments.author: selfish_meme
comments.body: I find a lot of stuff in Unreal Engine challenging, large landscapes and foliage, water and bouyancy, animation, writing as much in c++ before getting to that is helping, The game I started this week is almost complete gameplay, story, economy, characters, 9 levels 7 missions, but I have done no art for it yet, but I'm basically running soak tests constantly at 3x speed while programming and the computer is handling it fine

comments.author: lawlshawk
comments.body:
Systems-heavy games like roguelikes. Fun is a feeling... you can't always get there without a lot of playtesting and refinement.

  
Don't try to one-shot the whole game. Get the first 5-10 minutes feeling good, then build on it a piece at a time.

comments.author: Such--Balance
comments.body: I would say generally, the right 'feel' and level of challenge is still very hard for ai across the board

comments.author: Robonotes1760
comments.body:
From my experience, games with novel, complex mechanics. I was able to get GPT 5.1 (I think) through M365 Copilot last year to create a working Space Invaders clone in about 4 prompts in 2025; a novel reverse platformer (where the computer controls the "player" character and the actual player has to place enemies and traps to give the "player" a game over) took a week of intensive prompting with GPT 5.5/5.6 (and a lot of technical direction about how it should actually work).

The project on which I am working now, continuing development on Simutrans-Extended, is taking a very large amount of time and oversight *per feature*. Having worked on Simutrans-Extended for many years in the pre-AI days and having done little since about 2023, I resumed work on getting the planned features in the next version ready in about September this year, and am still going. I am working in my spare time, but a single feature change can sometimes take multiple evenings. A single bugfix once took two days. 

Although it is a game from the 1990s that has been open source since 2004 and although it is, broadly, in a well known historical genre, the actual direction that I have been taking with Simutrans-Extended since I first forked it in 2008 (hyper-realism on the economic dimension, at a huge scale, with maps roughly the size of England at 125 meters per tile) is entirely novel and highly complex.

On the one hand, AI has revolutionised the coding quality and throughput (I was self-taught in C++ specifically for working on this game, having no professional background in IT at all and the AI is finding and fixing a large number of bugs from before AI development started, as well as implementing a number of major performance optimisations). On the other hand, it still needs a lot of guidance and steering about what actually makes sense in the world of Simutrans-Extended.

I will give a recent example: waiting times. In Simutrans-Extended, which route that passengers/mail/goods take is based on overall journey time, which is divided into walking time, waiting time and travel time for each leg of the journey. Waiting times are calculated based on how long that mail/passengers/goods have actually waited at a stop before their transport takes them on the next leg of their journey. The waiting times of the last 32 packets of mail/passengers/goods are averaged. However, this then creates anomalies when a previously frequent service becomes infrequent; so we have to detect when the waiting times of *current* packets exceed the average waiting times by more than a factor of 2. This was all implemented as long ago as 2013 - but the AI found a bug to the effect that packets that had been waiting >2x the existing mean waiting time were being double counted at every check and again when they boarded their final transport, skewing the result. The AI was good at proposing the basic fix (add a boolean value per packet to check whether it had been counted before), but had to be prompted to give the most efficient version of this (re-use an existing not fully utilised bitfield rather than create a complete new 8-bit boolean value), which would make a real difference, since there are vast numbers of packets in the game when there is a large, developed transport network. Also, it initially proposed just using the maximum of the known mean or current recorded > 2x mean as the waiting time when the path explorer is finding routes, which would not be a sensible solution because it would involve treating what may be a temporary disruption as the only relevant information about waiting times; I had to prompt it specifically to choose the *mean* of the general mean and the current elevated amount as a more sensible choice.

Now imagine creating a game of this sort from the ground up and having to supply this level of granular detail about exact mechanisms and implementation for thousands upon thousands of individual development choices. This is why we are a very long way off from "Make me GTA VI" in one prompt.

comments.author: Zaflis
comments.body:
It needs to be taught to build many small modular systems. MMO is made out of several features that the map makers and game designers can use to piece together the game itself. AI can act as 1 of each 1 little problem at the time. It does not need to work on the thing as a whole before it has all the feature sets done individually and tested working.

"Make a 3D character animation, Add commands to create a creature, make it move, etc..."

replies.author: teapot_RGB_color
replies.body:
Exactly, and that why it is the hardest to develop, not only do you have to make many small modular systems, but you have to connect to all together at some point AND follow a united design / lore / convention.

And then still not break anything. There is so many points of failure here, which grows the more systems you put in place.

It really need a lot of planning and itteration, and I think for the time being that planning alone is out of scope for a small team (to match something like Skyrim or WoW)

comments.author: BigBossMemin
comments.body:
I would say any genre. If the scope is "big" it is hard. Im making a 2d horror game inspired by Darkwood. I had to define the architecture first to allow a scalable project and that's just for gameplay systems and it took me a lot of time to develop even with AI.

 For this game I still have to work on the story, level design, layout, pacing, tension and those are just few of many things that an AI is not very good at. Thats just my opinion and my experience with the way I've been working with claude code in Godot. But maybe I'm wrong and AI can do it and I just don't know how.

comments.author: Negative_Gur9667
comments.body: It could do most of the SFX mixing for me though. Ask me if you like.

replies.author: azzogat
replies.body:
Please do share. Have experimented with this in many ways. 

Generation of 1-2 sounds that are not terrible are the most I got out of ludo/ eleven labs and every automated workflow I tried has spectacularly failed.

replies.author: Negative_Gur9667
replies.body:
For SFX I let claude generate a soundboard with access to the elevenlabs api so I can make masses of sounds to try for each action ingame. I can promt new sounds directly into the sound board.

Then I let a limiter an compressor do the leveling and for the really shitty sounds I manually make them less loud inside the sound board.

For overly loud sounds I use sidechaining to duck the rest. Its really impressive.

I will show a demo of my game soon, I'm just waiting for my steam store acc to be validated.

replies.author: azzogat
replies.body:
This is more or less what I tried. Also tried with my ( fairly large and well organized ) SFX collections - which are generally higher quality than what Ludo/ EL can output currently.

It works for ambiance and even simple slow/ isolated sounds but trying to get more complicated  soundscapes going without enormous overlap, ducking the right ones, deciding priorities and adjusting for visual clarity has so far failed me. Even abusing all the usual tricks ( rng pitch, channel/ bank isolation ) still means enormous manual work and really bad results on my side.  Not even going to mention FX chains.

When you do have something to show, please, do share.

replies.author: Negative_Gur9667
replies.body:
Looking at your setup, you may want to set up an interface like in Ableton Live so you can group your sounds, lessen the complexity, and also take back control of the order of things by also copying the effects interface.

https://i.redd.it/qtjdrzinzf1i1.jpeg

comments.author: azzogat
comments.body:
I meant sound effects. We had much better results with VFX/ special effects. Not entirely automated workflows, but certainly decent results in 2D and particularly in frame-based VFX.

Not so much with particle based effects, especially in 3D, but I guess 3D is overall difficult for AI.

comments.author: alphapussycat
comments.body: Any genre with art, AI has not seen that much development in it.

replies.author: despacito6456
replies.body: dosent every genre have art

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body:
Exactly. And there is a reason it doesn't work. You can't one shot a backend, I tried 🤣
You can do a lot with a single prompt but it only goes so far. Sure you could have the whole game in one big file prompt but ai still won't succeed, because it needs you to tell good from bad and right from wrong.

comments.author: lifeiswe1rd
comments.body: Life simulation games. The detailed animations and facial animations are not AIs forte currently.

comments.author: OrangClive44
comments.body:
Two genres:

1. Horror. Horror is simply a very humanesque genre. Humans in general are not very good at writing horror stories not because they don't understand fear but because they don't understand how to create real tension between the reader/player and the game/environment. Most horror is done through shock rather than through narrative for this reason and AI tends to not do either of those things terribly well.

2. Strategy. Ironically AI is too good at strategy games to make a strategy game a human could play. It's sort of like how few humans can really beat a computer at chess now on the hardest difficulty we have for those programs. AI will optimize the strategy in a way that a human would never intuit because it's basically all of us as one; think of it like making a jumping puzzle for the average person by someone who solved Navier-Stokes and is using real physics to decipher exactly what should occur. 

Everything else kind of is okay; the number of real tools that existed prior to LLMs which helped with these genres is definitely non-zero and they have things like consistency checkers and stuff. So even if you get a soulless visual novel that isn't an LLM failure; it's just poor writing.

comments.author: Timely_Spirit_9053
comments.body: ive seen a lot of games, but one thing i havent seen yet is probably....huge games, unsure how it would work with games that have more players
